title: Inference, profiling and measured performance
outcome: Explain which work a timing includes, inspect type inference and measure a small kernel without turning machine-dependent timing into a correctness assertion.
key_terms: The compiler's deduction of result types from argument types, which `@inferred` checks against the observed result.
Julia compiles a separate method instance for each combination of concrete argument types it encounters.
Timing a call after an initial run so that compilation time is excluded from the reported cost.
Using `@allocated` to report the bytes an expression allocates, exposing temporaries or type instability.
Passing a value of uncertain type into a separate function so that function is compiled for the concrete type.
approach: Keep correctness and timing in separate claims. `sum_squares` is parametric in `T<:AbstractFloat` and starts at `zero(T)`, so its return type is inferable and matches the element type. `measured` calls the kernel once to compile it, then wraps a second call in `@timed` and returns the value, seconds and bytes, and only the value is asserted.

exercises.title: Trace the accumulator
exercises.answer: The accumulator is Float64 throughout; the final value is 14.
exercises.why: The loop adds 1 squared to reach 1, then 4 to reach 5, then 9 to reach 14, all as `Float64` because `zero(Float64)` started the total.
exercises.wrong: Adding the items before squaring gives 6 and then 36, which is the square of the sum rather than the sum of squares.
exercises.verify: Print `total` inside an owned copy of the loop and compare with `sum_squares([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) == 14`.

exercises.title: Preserve precision
exercises.hint: Inspect typeof as well as value.
exercises.answer: `zero(T)` and floating multiplication preserve the specified small-case element arithmetic.
exercises.why: With `T = Float32`, `zero(T)` and each product stay `Float32`, so the result is exactly `Float32(5)`.
exercises.wrong: Initializing `total = 0.0` promotes the sum to `Float64` and makes `@inferred` report a type other than the element type.

exercises.title: Change workload size
exercises.expected: Both return four times their length; observed time may vary.
exercises.hint: Do not assert which individual call is faster.
exercises.answer: A larger workload changes the experiment. Multiple observations are needed to compare scaling.
exercises.why: Every element of `fill(2.0, n)` contributes 4, so the value is 400 for length 100 and 40000 for length 10000.
exercises.wrong: Asserting that the longer run takes about 100 times longer turns a machine-dependent observation into a test that can fail randomly.
exercises.verify: Assert the two values, collect several `measured` observations per length and report their spread rather than one number.

exercises.title: Diagnose invalid science
exercises.task: Pass `[NaN]` and explain why inference still succeeds.
exercises.hint: A known type is not a finite value.
exercises.answer: Inference concerns types. Scientific input validation is a separate contract.
exercises.why: NaN is a `Float64`, so inference finds the same concrete type and the kernel returns NaN, since NaN times NaN is NaN.
exercises.wrong: Reading a clean `@code_warntype` report as proof that inputs are valid confuses type stability with data validation.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `sum_squares([NaN]) |> isnan` and `sum_squares([Inf]) == Inf`; add an explicit `isfinite` check where needed.

exercises.title: Design a benchmark record
exercises.task: List the fields needed to reproduce a timing claim.
exercises.expected: Include input, versions, threads, cold/warm boundary and repetitions.
exercises.hint: Keep correctness results with the timings.
exercises.answer: A benchmark record identifies environment and work; a number without these cannot support a transferable claim.
exercises.why: A timing is reproducible only if the record names the input size, Julia version, thread count, warm or cold state and the number of repeats.
exercises.wrong: Publishing a single `@time` line from a laptop gives readers no way to tell whether compilation or other load was included.
exercises.verify: Store the correctness check result beside each timing row and rerun the record on another machine to compare.

exercises.title: Transfer to a data pipeline
exercises.task: Identify which parsing, fitting and plotting boundaries you would measure.
exercises.answer: Phase measurements explain bottlenecks while end-to-end time captures the actual user experience.
exercises.why: Timing parsing, fitting and plotting separately locates the slow phase, while one outer timer measures what a user waits for.
exercises.wrong: Adding the phase times to an outer timer that already contains them counts each phase twice.
exercises.verify: Check that the phase times sum to less than or equal to the end-to-end time and explain any gap.
